Am I right in understanding my friend to suggest that the committee should be restricted to matters which come exclusively under the federal parliament and over which the provinces have no jurisdiction?
Mr. BOURA'SSA:	I think a clear distinction should be made in the committee. It seems to me that the duty of the representative of the government in that committee would be, the moment a question cropped tip affecting provincial rights or jurisdiction, to point cut to the committee the uselessness of wasting time on its discussion. For example, if the question of the Senate were raised, I think it would be the duty of that representative and of every member of this parliament possessed of the spirit of confederation to remind the committee that the Senate is not to 'be judged only according to the good or bad votes it gives on this or that measure, but according to the spirit of the institution, according to those principles of confederation which my friend wants to preserve. But c-f course, once a clear definition were made, the whole matter should be submitted to the inter-provincial conference. I think it would clarify the situation and enable both the representatives of the federal par-
B.N.A. Act-Amendment

liament and the representatives of the provincial legislatures to accomplish some work.
As to the argument made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Guthrie) that there is no need for any change in our constitution, I cannot agree. There may not be a crying need for radical changes; but let us remember that having to live under a written constitution is in itself a great inconvenience. We have not the advantage that the people of Great Britain have of being able to reshape their constitution from time to time according to their needs. The constitution of Great. Britain is in a constant process of evolution and reshaping, and therefore grows with the people; while we have outgrown many parts of our constitution. As regards our relations with the British government, it may be that we still have in this House and in the country men with the colonial spirit of a hundred years ago who consider that we should make no change in those relations. For example, with respect to the power of disallowance. Well, I would respectfully give those men the same advice that I have given to certain Catholic friends of mine-not to be more Catholic than the Pope; I would advise those men not to take a narrower and more English view of these things than that held by all the leading men of Great Britain. When public men in England hear colonials saying that we do not want to grow nationally, they look upon us as inferior beings and conclude that we have not the strength of will and the power of mind to live out our own national life as they have taught us to do on the other side of the ocean.

subtopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Does not the
hon. gentleman think that in view of the fact of our two jurisdictions, provincial and federal, we will always require a written constitution to define their respective limits?

subtopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Of course. Even if we were completely independent-as I think we will be, one of these days-we will have a written constitution, just as the Americans have. But the Americans have made their constitution grow with their national growth. Take the role of the Supreme Court of the United States with regard to the constitution and compare some of its decisions in Washington sixty years ago with those rendered to-day, for example, that famous decision which held that under the constitution a slave-owner was just as much master of the body of his slave as he was of his ox or his ass. I do not think the Supreme Court of the United States would render such a judgment to-day. Then take the various decisions handed down by that court after the conquest of Porto Rico and the annexation
(Mr. Bourassa.]
of the Philippines, and you will find how the court enlarged the scope of the American constitution in order to deal with the new problems that had arisen with the growth of the American nation. So long as we do not assert our right to deal with our own affairs in our own way; so long as we do not regard the Supreme Court of Canada as the ultimate tribunal to interpret the constitution of this country; so long as we do not consider this parliament the supreme authority in giving expression to the will of the Canadian people, just so long shall we be handicapped by that narrow colonial spirit which renders us inferior to the people of Great Britain.
With regard to the other point raised by the leader of the opposition concerning minority rights, I entirely agree with the Minister of Justice. Just as, speaking as a Canadian and a British citizen, I cannot stand the idea of colonial inferiority, neither can I, as a French Canadian and a Catholic, tolerate the idea that we need have recourse to a foreign power to protect us. Of course I admit that there might be some risk, but surely we French Canadians have proven in three hundred years that we are manly enough to face risks. I must say, speaking my own mind, that I am unable to agree altogether with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) in the view that English speaking Canadians generally are as broadminded as Englishmen at home. Unfortunately they are not, and we have had many proofs to this effect. But I believe that the more responsibility the people of Canada at large exercise, English or French, Catholic or Protestant, the less they rely upon outside authority to correct their misdemeanours or to prevent them from doing foolish things, the more will their sense of responsibility increase and the more broadminded will they become. We are absolutely the masters of our constitution; there is no doubt of that. But so long as we do not exercise the power that is ours in that respect, it remains dormant and circumscribed. We must exercise it, and no one will be more glad to see us assert ourselves than the powers that be in England, because they have enough to do to look after their own affairs without being obliged to settle our small quarrels in Canada. They do not care to adjust matters between Catholic and Protestant, French or English in this country. It is not their business to do so and they do not want to have the responsibility. The English had to deal with the Irish for seven centuries and they have had enough of that sort of thing. The Irish made it quite evident that it was absurd for Englishmen to want to rule a foreign people from

B.N.A. Act-Amendment
the English point of view. It seems to me that both English speaking and French speaking Canadians, whether Catholic or Protestant, will settle their differences more satisfactorily when they confer solely among themselves, in absolute freedom.
As regards the federal pact, I have expressed the view, time and again in Quebec, and I repeat it on this occasion, that if that pact holds good, it holds good in Ottawa as well as in London. If it is broken in Ottawa, or Toronto, or anywhere else in Canada, the king will not send a regiment to this country to make the pact good in favour of French Canadians or of Catholics. It may be that some of the hon. gentlemen surrounding the leader of the opposition would be prepared to raise the banner of King William to save us Catholics from Protestant domination, but I do not quite expect that.
I rather rely on the common sense of the vast majority of English speaking Protestant Canadians. I do not think it is the proper spirit to foster in this country, to make English speaking Canadians believe that if it were not for the maternal protection of Great Britain we could be wiped out. Do not let anybody remain under that delusion. We cannot be wiped out; and if the English speaking Canadians could wipe us out the vast majority of them would not do so. Of course, at election times, once in a while, a certain number of people are bound to talk that way-one flag, one language, and so forth. But when it comes to a matter of practice, every reasonable man knows that two and a half million French Canadians are not going to be turned into English speaking people. On the contrary, we are freely learning English because we want to communicate with the rest of Canada and we want to prove to them that we do not suffer from that incapacity referred to a short time ago, of not being intelligent enough to acquire a second language. Those English speaking Canadians who suggest that this opinion is held generally throughout Canada simply calumniate their own people.
The more we have to discuss between ourselves matters of the kind that are called burning questions, dangerous questions, the more we consider them together as between man and man, the more will there grow up in Canada a proper spirit of conciliation, and the more courage will evidence itself on both sides, however much prejudice there may be at times. And of course prejudices are bound to exist. The discussion may be heated at times, but finally difficulties will have to be adjusted as they were adjusted in 1867. Conciliation was the spirit of confederation.
Cartier and Macdonald did not go to London to seek advice on how to deal with the school question or with the question of minority rights or anything else. They first secured George Brown and gagged him with a portfolio; they silenced him for a few years. He was the only man who raised any trouble in those days, for the good old Tory party was unanimous at that time for the protection of French Catholics. As I say, they gagged George Brown, and that was Cartier's masterpiece; because, as Macdonald said in some of his letters, "I cannot speak with the man." He therefore used Cartier as an intermediary; diplomatist as he was, he used a French-Canadian for the purpose. Thus it was that, after Brown was brought in, confederation was made possible.
What were the outstanding principles of confederation? In the first place, the whole of Canada in becoming a self-governing country was asserting its right to full fledged autonomy. As everybody knows, Sir John Macdonald wanted the Dominion to be called the Kingdom of Canada. We have evidence, not only in his letters but in his public utterances, that he wanted to entertain with foreign powers such relations as we are beginning to establish to-day. Everyone knows that he was absolutely opposed to any kind or form of contribution by the people of Canada to any war waged by England outside Canada. We have testimony to this effect all through his life, in all his actions. The second principle of confederation was that in every province of Canada, the minority, French or English, Protestant or Catholic, should enjoy exactly the same rights in matters of language and of sohools. We have stood by the agreement on both points, and we are prepared to stand by it in complete amity with the other peoples of the Dominion. As Canadians, we are prepared to discuss the problems that confront us without the interference of a tribunal in London oir of any body responsible to the electors of Yorkshire or of Midlothian. We are ready to settle our own affairs without reference to any suoh outside authority as to whether we should insert or omit a comma here or there in our constitutioh, or eliminate a sentence or half a sentence elsewhere.
It behooves us to assert-what was acknowledged unanimously this summer by representatives of all the self-governing countries of the empire-that Canada has the right and the power to deal with her own constitution just as freely as Great Britain can deal with hers. And inasmuch as oura is a written constitution, the result of a contract between two races, an agreement among
B.N.A. Act-Amendment

several provinces; inasmuch as there are new provinces which did not exist at the time of confederation, and new problems which did not then present themselves: in view of these circumstances it seems to me that the two processes, advocated respectively by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) and by the Minister of Justice, instead of conflicting with each other, are rather complementary. I think my friends on the other side should acknowledge that anything done or said in this House cannot close the matter, and that the provinces must pronounce themselves as political bodies and political entities within the confederacy, just as the provinces have no right and no power to prevent this House from doing anything we desire to do in our federal affairs or from making such suggestions as we may think are for the benefit of Canada.
It seems to me that there would jbe no time lost, because our constitution cannot be amended as the'English constitution is amended in fact- from day to day. Once in a while we have to put it on the "metier", as we say in French, to see whether it has been outgrown, whether it should be added to or modified, and this should be done periodically. We should have a committee to look after the revision of the constitution let us say every 'ten years. Instead of waiting until there is discontent and until the various parts of the country begin to bicker, it would be a good thing to look after it from time to time, Therefore in that spirit and with those reservations, while agreeing entirely with the Minister of Justice in the main portion of his argument, it seems to me that the motion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre could be accepted in that broad spirit, with the desire to accomplish something more comprehensive and more practical than a mere inter-provincial conference could bring about by itself, without having received first of all an indication of the opinion of this parliament.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. H. CAHAN (St. Lawrence-St. George):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to
enter upon this discussion, but I think it discloses the fact that once you begin to make shreds and patches of the constitution, either of Great Britain in her relations to the dominions or of the dominions themselves in relation to their separate provinces or states, you at once open a large field for discussion in which we may reach no satisfactory conclusion, and are indeed incapable of doing so. The constitution of a country is on an entirely different basis from the ordinary statutes and enactments of parliament; a con-

stitution is made not for the present but for the far-reaching future. It must necessarily change and be subject to modifications, but the matter of modification or change must be approached1 in an entirely different spirit from that in which we would consider the amendment of a mere statute dealing with commercial, corporation or criminal law.
I do not suffer, and I do not think members of this parliament or the people of this country suffer, from any inferiority complex; I believe the electors of this country are as intelligent, if not more intelligent, than are on the whole the electors of Great Britain and Ireland. I know something of Scotland and something of England; and in my opinion the majority of the electors of those countries are not more intelligent than are the average of the electors of our own country. I do not think the lawyers of Canada suffer from any inferiority complex; I meet the best lawyers of London from time to time as well as those of New York and Washington, and I have never felt that I could not safeguard the interests of my clients in dealing with them quite as satisfactorily as I can safeguard the interests of my clients in dealing with the lawyers of Toronto, Edmonton or Vancouver.
I do not think we suffer in Canada from the colonial spirit; if that spirit exists in this country I do not know where it exists. I do not find it in the eastern provinces or in Quebec, and I certainly do not find it in the west; so that any discussion of the colonial spirit seems to me entirely apart from the question. If the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has really made up his mind that the independence of Canada is necessary to the welfare of the country as a whole and that it should be achieved within a short time,
I can understand why he should openly advocate our independence as he has done this afternoon. Unfortunately, he does not conceive that the members of this House or the people of this country may advocate the continuance of their political relations to the British throne and to Great Britain and Ireland and the other great dominions, except that it be advocated by reason of an inferiority complex or through being permeated1 with a colonial spirit. I take an entirely different view. I look to Canada to develop and1 to become one of the great nations of the world. If I or you, Mr. Speaker, could return to this country fifty or sixty or one hundred years hence, we would1 see a progress and development in Canada in every department of national life which would surpass the highest anticipations of the people of to-day. It is bound to come, but I believe it will best be

B.N.A. Act-Amendment
achieved if we make no sudden break and have no sudden cleavage from the traditions under which we were born and bred, and which are an inspiration to the great body of our people both French and English. These traditions were not traditions) of servility. They were never such in the province of Quebec even in the rural districts of that province, and are not such to-day; there is no spirit of servility there. Although the hon. member has had far more experience from his associations with the people of that province than I possess, yet I believe that though they have not a spirit of servility, and while they are not permeated with the colonial spirit, the great body of those people are willing and anxious to maintain those ancient and honourable liens which, bind the people of Canada to the British throne, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the other great dominions beyond the seas. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that they are not ready to disrupt and tear up the ties or liens of the constitutional fabric which binds us to the rest of the British Commonwealth to-day.

speechtext:
I accept that statement from the hon. member for Labelle, but I thought that some phrases which he used or statements which he made went beyond that. It seems to me that the great object of the people in Canada to-day, both of the east and west and of the centre, should be to develop a unity of national sentiment, to develop, if you will, a common speech in the use of both languages; because I believe that a knowledge of the French language is absolutely necessary to a thorough knowledge and appreciation of the mentality and high character of the great body of people of the province in which I represent a constituency. We must achieve that spirit of national unity before we will be in a position to discuss in the
future any dissolution of those ties which bind us to the other British dominions and to the British throne.
Now, in connection with that problem, any proposal for a revision of the British North America Act, as suggested, will, I think, create a considerable degree of suspicion. It will meet a very considerable degree of suspicion in the eastern provinces of Canada; it will meet possibly, among the thoughtful men of the west, the same degree of suspicion and reluctance to enter upon any new constitutional arrangement of a radical character or quality. We must first apply ourselves to achieving that unity, and even those who look forward to the independence of Canada must for years devote their intellectual energies to preparing Canada for that breach if inevitably it is to come. We must -and I intend to discuss this under another resolution, namely, the matter of appeals to the Privy Council-we must perfect the machinery of our own courts of justice. We must give to our own Supreme court a higher standing, and create greater confidence in its decisions on the part of the people of this country before we can abrogate the right of appeal to the Privy Council. I think I have read most of the discussions as reported in shorthand of the arguments before the Privy Council dealing with our own constitutional affairs; and, as I said the other day in committee, it is only occasionally that we see glimpses of intelligence on the part of members of the Judicial Committee, when dealing with t'he local affairs of the Dominion of Canada, yet I confess that the people have not sufficient confidence in our own Supreme court to-day to abrogate entirely not only appeals in criminal cases, appeals in commercial cases, but appeals in constitutional cases; and, although the province of Quebec has met with many disappointments in respect of appeals to the Privy Council, yet I am persuaded that the great body of intelligent opinion in that province is, for the time being and under present conditions, that the light of appeal in constitutional cases should still be maintained. There is a feeling that, if the right of appeal in constitutional cases is not maintained, our people will not have the same confidence in the decisions of our own Supreme Court of Canada as at present constituted; and until you have, on the part of the people of all the provinces, implicit confidence in the ability, in the intelligence, and in the impartiality of our own Supreme court, you would introduce an element of discord, of suspicion and misapprehension into
B.N.A. Act-Amendment

the minds of the people of this country, if you were to abolish at the present time the right of appeal to the Privy Council in constitutional cases.
And then where is the need to-day of any radical revision of the British North America Act? The moment you begin to revise the British North America Act in its essential particulars you place the whole structure, it seems to me, in the melting pot; and we are not prepared to-day to have it placed in the melting pot and to set about arranging a new contract or agreement between the provinces as a basis for a new constitution for this country. Our constitution is different, as the hon. member for Labelle has said, from the constitutions of South Africa, of New Zealand, or of Australia. We are in this country a people drawn originally from two races. It took from 1791 until 1867 to reach a compact or agreement between those two races as to the terms on which they were prepared to cooperate and live in unity for the future; and if you now wipe out that compact, if you now put it into the melting pot, you introduce into Canada an element of discord, which will prevent this country from giving the time and attention it should give to its material and social development. If there were any grave evils apparent I would say let us adjust those evils. Certainly there is no difference between the status of the three provinces of the middle west and that of the provinces of the east which calls for placing the whole constitution in the melting pot to-day. The sole difference between the constitutions of Saskatchewan and Alberta and the constitution of Ontario, is the one provision with regard to natural resources and subsidies; and there was a body of opinion in the territories in 1905, which was represented by some of the ablest and most thoughtful men that we had produced in Canada at that time. They became parties to an arrangement which was carried into effect by the constitutional acts of Alberta and Saskatchewan of 1905, and they decided then that it was to their advantage that the natural resources of those new provinces should be held by the crown in the right of the Dominion of Canada, and that those provinces should receive in compensation annual subsidies largely increased in amount. To-day, Mr. Speaker, if those provinces wish their natural resources back there is not a voice in this House that will be raised against giving them back, by transferring to the crown in right of the provinces these parts of the natural resources which are not yet appropriated. The sole issue is not with regard to the return of the natural 
resources to Alberta, but as to certain portions of the natural resources-of the lands, mines, and forests,-which have been appropriated by the parliament of Canada for the purposes of carrying out certain educational trusts. To-day not a member of this House, I believe, would stand up and vote against the transfer of the natural resources to Alberta or to Saskatchewan; but we simply ask, some of us, that with respect to those lands already appropriated for educational purposes, the terms and conditions of that trust should be maintained and carried out by the crown in the right of the provinces as it is now being carried out by the crown in the right of the Dominion. Therefore there is no serious consideration presented to us why we should put our constitution in the melting pot because of any grave difference of status between the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan on the one hand, and the provinces of the east on the other.
Is there any subject which for the general advantage of Canada should be dealt with by the parliament of Canada, but which parliament now has not complete jurisdiction to deal with? There may be some, but I do not know of any. There is a question arising in the province of Ontario which we have been discussing in the special committee, as to the powers of the provincial legislature and the powers of our own parliament respectively, in imposing restrictions and conditions upon the operations of loan companies. Why should not the province have the right to deal with and prescribe the conditions under which certain insurance companies or certain loan companies should operate within its borders? That is certainly not a matter which calls for the placing of the constitution of this country into the melting pot again. Those are questions which for sixty years have been successfully dealt with by the courts of this country, and which will be so dealt with again during the next sixty years. Therefore, it seems to me, without taking the time of this House, that the one aim and object of all of us who desire to promote the interests of Canadian nationality, as I do, should be to secure such conciliatory cooperation between the various parts of the Dominion that we, whenever an occasion may arise in future, may so understand the sentiment of each other and be so animated by the same purpose that we will work cordially together to promote and preserve the national interests of Canada in whatever form and from whatever source those interests may be attacked. That is not evidence of a colonial spirit. So far as the legislative control by the British

parliament is concerned it is merely at present a convenient form through which the parliament and legislatures of Canada may give expression (to their unanimous approval of certain projected changes or modifications in the Confederation act. It is simply a form of procedure, and before we abolish that form it is absolutely necessary that we should enter into a new compact, between the people of Canada on the one hand and ithe legislatures and people of each province on the other, that hereafter the constitution of Canada may be changed but may only be changed with the unanimous approval of the whole of the people, as represented by these legislatures.

That would afford us the opportunity for saying that we control and are masters of our own constitution, and that we may make it or amend it or modify it as we see fit. But the fact remains that by the same approval of all the legislatures, and by the approval of the parliament of Canada, we may to-day amend it as we see fit, and therefore for the purpose of providing a new form of procedure which might be gratifying to our national pride, in the present condition of sentiment in this country, when there is lack of complete unanimity, we should not, I think, place the existing constitution into the melting pot for the purpose of arriving at a new compact which should provide the same necessary conditions, the consent of all the provinces to any proposed amendments or modifications. The time is not ripe for it. The time may come in twenty years, or it may come in thirty years or in a century. The main object of members of this parliament and of our people should be to prepare ourselves so that when that time necessarily comes we shall have such unanimity of political sentiment in this country as will enable us as a united people to go on and fulfil our destiny as a great Canadian nation on the northern 'half of this continent, prepared to stand for political rights, to fight our way, to maintain our liberty in spite of any aggression from any other part of the world. But do not let us be premature about it. Do not let us undertake the consideration of these grave constitutional changes until we are actually forced by circumstances to do so. Any country that has ever developed constitutionally has done so by producing men who are able, qualified and competent to deal with any such crisis as it arises. Then, when a crisis does arise, when you are actually forced into effecting these constitutional amendments, you have the men to 32649-67

The sentiments expressed by the hon. member who spoke lost (Mr. Cahan) seemed to me to be typical of the statesmen that we have had governing this country for many years-they do not want to deal with any problem until it is forced upon them. I think it is time we looked upon our problems in a different way and said, "We see this problem in the distance; we will start now to study it and perhaps we can reach a solution of it sooner and in a more satisfactory manner."
My only reason for taking part in this debate was to remind the House of the circumstances under which confederation was accomplished. There were several provinces in Canada-they were not really provinces, but each one was a colony. The representatives of these colonies came together, sat around a council table and considered the question:	"Is there any agreement which
we could enter into with the object of forming a dominion out of all these colonies?" Four of these colonies voluntarily entered confederation. They were the charter members. Prince Edward Island I think was a colony at that time by itself. It could have come [DOT] into the union, but it said: "The terms offered to us are not satisfactory, and we will remain out." They afterwards came in of their own volition and on an agreement satisfactory to them. Later on British Columbia came in, on certain terms which were granted to her. She was not forced in, but I think Canada agreed to build a railway to British Columbia to induce her to come in. Then these provinces or colonies which were formed into the Dominion of Canada afterwards created other so-called provinces out of the great prairies lying in western Canada. I say "so-called," because if these colonies had been made into real provinces they would have been given the rights that were enjoyed by other provinces that came into the confederation. These western provinces, in my opinion, have been held by the rest of Canada very much in the same manner as Spain, Britain and other nations have held their colonies in the past. If these western provinces had been treated the same as the other provinces of Canada, after they had been formed into provinces, they would have been given the opportunity to say whether or not they wanted to come into confederation. speechtext: May I ask whether the hon. gentleman has read the debates in this House of 1905, on the Autonomy Bill, when the feelings of the people of western Canada were expressed (through their representatives on that question?

speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I have not, and it seems to me it would not very greatly alter the facts with which I am dealing. I do not think those representatives were entitled to speak for provinces which were not then formed.

subtopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext: They were entitled to speak for the territories out of which the provinces were formed.

subtopic: PROPOSED SPECIAL COMMITTEE TO CONSIDER AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
My contention is that these provinces should have exactly the same rights as the other provinces which entered confederation, and the other provinces all had the right to sit down at the council table and say on what terms they would come in.
I want to conclude before six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and before sitting down I just wish to say that I am heartily in favour of this resolution. I think, if the committee were formed and discussed this question, the government would know very well what was the attitude of parliament in regard to many of these questions which must be considered largely from a Dominion point of view, and our representatives would then enter the interprovincial conference with that opinion of the House to guide them in their deliberations.
On motion of Mr. Mareil the debate was adjourned.
At six o'clock the House adjourned, without question being put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, March 10, 1927
